claim: Type I SGNs represent 90–95% of the total SGN population.
source: Type I SGNs represent 90–95% of the total SGN population, form monosynaptic contacts with individual inner HCs (IHCs), and facilitate the majority of all hearing function.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript providing a specific quantitative range for type I SGN representation.

claim: Type I SGNs form monosynaptic contacts with individual inner hair cells.
source: Type I SGNs represent 90–95% of the total SGN population, form monosynaptic contacts with individual inner HCs (IHCs), and facilitate the majority of all hearing function.
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the synaptic connectivity pattern of type I SGNs.

claim: Type I SGNs facilitate the majority of all hearing function.
source: Type I SGNs represent 90–95% of the total SGN population, form monosynaptic contacts with individual inner HCs (IHCs), and facilitate the majority of all hearing function.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the functional role of type I SGNs.

claim: Type II SGNs comprise 5–10% of the SGN population.
source: Type II SGNs comprise the remaining 5–10% of the SGN population, and, in contrast with Type I SGNs, bypass the IHCs to form en passant synapses with up to 10 outer HCs (OHCs) per individual SGN fiber (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement providing a specific quantitative range for type II SGN representation.

claim: Type II SGNs bypass IHCs to form en passant synapses with up to 10 outer hair cells per individual SGN fiber.
source: Type II SGNs comprise the remaining 5–10% of the SGN population, and, in contrast with Type I SGNs, bypass the IHCs to form en passant synapses with up to 10 outer HCs (OHCs) per individual SGN fiber (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the synaptic connectivity pattern of type II SGNs, with reference to Figure 1A for visual support.

claim: Type II SGNs are not myelinated by neural crest-derived Schwann cells that myelinate type I SGNs.
source: In addition, type II SGNs are not myelinated by the neural crest derived-Schwann cells that myelinate type I SGNs (Carney and Silver, 1983; Breuskin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Type II SGNs may facilitate responses to very loud or painful sounds.
source: Although their function is not well understood, recent landmark studies have suggested that type II SGNs may facilitate responses to very loud or painful sounds (Weisz et al., 2009, 2012, 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: SGNs show differences in protein expression and firing rates that correlate with their location along the tonotopic axis.
source: SGNs also show differences in protein expression and firing rates that correlate with their location along the tonotopic axis (Flores-Otero et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: Type I fibers can be sub-divided into two groups based on spontaneous firing rates and synaptic location at the base of individual IHCs.
source: Finally, type I fibers can be sub-divided into two groups based on spontaneous firing rates and synaptic location at the base of individual IHCs (Liberman, 1982).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by a citation.

claim: SGN processes do not enter the cochlear epithelium until hair cells begin to differentiate.
source: SGN processes do not enter the epithelium until HCs being to differentiate (E14.5 base) but then rapidly extend towards the developing IHCs (C–E).
evidence: This statement is supported by cross-sectional images in Figure 1C-E showing temporal correlation between HC differentiation and SGN process entry.

claim: At E13.5, prior to detectable expression of Atoh1, SGN processes are present outside of the duct but do not yet project into the cochlear epithelium.
source: At embryonic day 13.5 (E13.5), prior to detectable expression of Atoh1, SGN processes are present outside of the duct, but do not yet project into the cochlear epithelium (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: By E14.5, SGN processes have entered the epithelium at the more mature base of the cochlea while remaining outside in less mature, more mid-modiolar regions.
source: By one day later (E14.5), processes have entered the epithelium at the more mature base of the cochlea while remaining outside in less mature, more mid-modiolar regions (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Neurite entry correlates with the onset of Atoh1 expression in developing hair cells.
source: Neurite entry correlates with the onset of Atoh1 expression in developing HCs (Figure 1E; arrow).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At E15.5, the ratio of SGN processes projecting towards the emerging OHC region appears to be closer to 50:50 than to the mature ratio of 5:95.
source: At E15.5, the ratio of SGN processes projecting towards the emerging OHC region appears to be closer to 50:50 than to the mature ratio of 5:95 (Figure 1F,G; see arrowheads).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: At E16.5, a noticeably higher concentration of processes appears around the IHC region.
source: However, at E16.5, a noticeably higher concentration of processes appears around the IHC region (Figure 1H; see arrowheads).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: SGNs may assume a type I- or type II-like morphology as early as E16.5.
source: These data suggest that the SGNs may assume a type I- or type II-like morphology as early as E16.5, which is both consistent with the time period of hair and supporting cell maturation and earlier than previously suggested.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 1, representing an inference from the observed patterns.

claim: Approximately 10–15 individual SGN peripheral axons project to each IHC.
source: Approximately, 10–15 individual SGN peripheral axons project to each IHC, making analysis of changes in individual fibers difficult (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the innervation pattern, supported by Figure 1I.

claim: At E15.5 in the mid-point along the cochlea, approximately 60% of individual SGN fibers terminated in the IHC region while the remaining 40% extended into the OHC region.
source: At the mid-point along the cochlea at E15.5, approximately 60% of individual SGN fibers terminated in the IHC region while the remaining 40% extended into the OHC region (Figure 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data shown in Figure 2A,B,E.

claim: In a more basal region of the E15.5 cochlea, the number of fibers terminating in the IHC and OHC regions was roughly equivalent.
source: However, in a more basal region of the same cochlea, the number of fibers terminating in the IHC and OHC regions was roughly equivalent (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At E17.5 or 18.5, between 70 to 80% of all labeled processes were apposed to IHCs.
source: In contrast, at E17.5 or 18.5, between 70 to 80% of all labeled processes were apposed to IHCs (Figure 2C–E), suggesting that a progressive transition to the mature innervation pattern begins shortly after E15.5.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: A progressive transition to the mature innervation pattern begins shortly after E15.5.
source: In contrast, at E17.5 or 18.5, between 70 to 80% of all labeled processes were apposed to IHCs (Figure 2C–E), suggesting that a progressive transition to the mature innervation pattern begins shortly after E15.5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal changes in innervation patterns observed in the data.

claim: At P0 and through P3, approximately 90–95% of all labeled SGNs fibers terminated in the IHC region with the remaining 5–10% extending into the OHC region.
source: Consistent with this trend, at P0 and through P3, approximately 90–95% of all labeled SGNs fibers terminated in the IHC region with the remaining 5–10% extending into the OHC region (Figure 2E; see also Figure 1J,K).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 1J,K.

claim: In the basal half of the cochlea at E16.5 and E17.5, between 4 and 19 CC3-positive SGNs were detected per cochlea.
source: In the basal half of the cochlea at these stages, where most of our neuronal-tracing experiments were performed, we detected between 4 and 19 CC3-positive SGNs per cochlea.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the apoptosis analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the apex of the cochlea at E16.5 and E17.5, between 18 and 50 CC3-positive SGNs were observed per cochlea.
source: At the apex, between 18 and 50 CC3-positive SGNs were observed per cochlea.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the apoptosis analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of SGNs is estimated to be greater than twenty thousand at E16.5-E17.5.
source: Given that the number of SGNs is estimated to be greater than twenty thousand at this stage (Richter et al., 2011), a role for apopotic cell death in SGN innervation at this stage seems unlikely.
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A role for apoptotic cell death in SGN innervation at E16.5-E17.5 seems unlikely.
source: Given that the number of SGNs is estimated to be greater than twenty thousand at this stage (Richter et al., 2011), a role for apopotic cell death in SGN innervation at this stage seems unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low number of apoptotic cells relative to the total SGN population.

claim: Time-lapse imaging indicated numerous instances of SGN processes that extended into the OHC region and then retracted back into the IHC region.
source: Analysis of time-lapse videos indicated numerous instances of SGN processes that extended into the OHC region and then retracted back into the IHC region or that were present in the OHC region at the beginning of the experiment and then retracted (Figure 2F; Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging experiments shown in Figure 2F and Video 1.

claim: 10–60% of the axons that started in the OHC region had retracted by the end of the time-lapse acquisition period.
source: We quantified this effect for axons in four independent time-lapse experiments and found that 10–60% of the axons that started in the OHC region had retracted by the end of the acquisition period (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from time-lapse imaging experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Many SGN peripheral axons initially extend into the OHC region but subsequently retract to form connections with IHCs.
source: Overall, these data indicate that many SGN peripheral axons initially extend into the OHC region but subsequently retract to form connections with IHCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Most SGNs have determined their phenotype (type I vs type II) by the late embryonic period or just shortly after birth.
source: Moreover, these results suggest that most SGNs have determined their phenotype (type I vs type II) by the late embryonic period or just shortly after birth (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal patterns of innervation observed in the data.

claim: Nrp2 is expressed in whole cochleae at E16.5.
source: Moreover, our previous unpublished studies using RT-PCR demonstrated that Neuropilin-2 (Nrp2) is expressed in whole cochleae at E16.5.
evidence: This is a statement about unpublished data from the authors.

claim: At E14.5, Nrp2 is detectable in the SGNs, but not in surrounding mesenchyme or epithelial tissues.
source: At E14.5, Nrp2 was detectable in the SGNs, but not in surrounding mesenchyme or epithelial tissues (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: At E16.5, Nrp2 is clearly detectable in the somata and peripheral axons of the SGNs.
source: At E16.5, when SGNs develop region-specific innervation patterns, Nrp2 is clearly detectable in the somata and peripheral axons of the SGNs (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The Nrp2 antibody labeled all of the SGN cell bodies.
source: The Nrp2 antibody labeled all of the SGN cell bodies, which suggests Nrp2 is expressed by all SGNs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data.

claim: Nrp2 is expressed by all SGNs.
source: The Nrp2 antibody labeled all of the SGN cell bodies, which suggests Nrp2 is expressed by all SGNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that all SGN cell bodies were labeled.

claim: Nrp2 was visible along all putative type I and II SGN endings at E18.5.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, Nrp2 was visible along all putative type I and II SGN endings in cross-sections at E18.5 (Figure 3E,F) and in whole-mount preparations at P0 (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: While cross-sections from P0 and P5 cochleae indicated persistent expression of Nrp2 protein in SGN somata, the overall intensity of staining was substantially reduced by comparison with earlier time points.
source: Interestingly, while cross-sections from P0 and P5 cochleae indicated persistent expression of Nrp2 protein in SGN somata, the overall intensity of staining was substantially reduced by comparison with the earlier time points (not shown).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data.

claim: Sema3F-Fc showed substantial binding to SGNs along the basal-to-apical axis of the cochlea at P0.
source: In contrast with control Fc, which showed little to no binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D), Sema3F-Fc showed substantial binding to SGNs along the basal-to-apical axis of the cochlea (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H; see arrows).
evidence: This is a direct observation from Fc-binding assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sema3F-Fc was detectable on neurofilament-positive structures consistent with the position of peripheral axons of both type I and II SGNs.
source: Similar to the anti-Nrp2 antibody staining in Figure 3E–H, Sema3F-Fc was detectable on neurofilament-positive structures that are consistent with the position of peripheral axons of both type I and II SGNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I–P).
evidence: This is a direct observation from Fc-binding assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I-P.

claim: Functional forms of Nrp2 are present on both type I and II SGNs.
source: These data suggest that functional forms of Nrp2 are present on both type I and II SGNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Sema3F-Fc binding data.

claim: In Nrp2−/− cochleae at E15.5, there were large bundles of SGN processes that extended into the OHC region, with far fewer processes terminating near the IHC region.
source: In contrast, in Nrp2−/− cochleae at E15.5, there were large bundles of SGN processes that extended into the OHC region, with far fewer processes terminating near the IHC region (Figure 3L–N).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data in Nrp2 mutant mice shown in Figure 3L-N.

claim: Changes in SGN patterning in Nrp2−/− mutants were not a result of a decrease in the total number of SGNs.
source: These changes were not a result of a decrease in the total number of SGNs, as quantifying SGN somata density indicated no differences between WT and Nrp2−/− cochleae (Figure 3O).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from SGN counting data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: Synaptotagmin-1 antibodies label the SGN afferent axons but do not mark olivocochlear efferents.
source: Since both are labeled by pan-neuronal markers such as neurofilament or beta-III-tubulin (Tuj1), we screened over a dozen antibodies against known neuronal factors and found that synaptotagmin-1 (Syt-1) antibodies label the SGN afferent axons but do not mark olivocochlear efferents (Figure 3P–T).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 3P-T.

claim: Both Nrp2+/− and Nrp2−/− cochleae show significant increases in the number of crossing fibers at E16.5.
source: Results indicate significant increases in the number of crossing fibers in both Nrp2+/− and Nrp2−/− cochleae (Figure 3U).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from Syt-1 labeling data shown in Figure 3U.

claim: Nrp2 plays a role in limiting the number of SGN axons that cross into the OHC region.
source: These data are consistent with a model in which Nrp2 plays a role in limiting the number of SGN axons that cross into the OHC region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotype in Nrp2 mutant mice.

claim: Phenotypic defects in midline commissural axon path finding have been reported in Nrp2+/− mice.
source: However, phenotypic defects in midline commissural axon path finding have been reported in Nrp2+/− mice, suggesting that heterozygosity for Nrp2 can lead to a significant decrease in Nrp2 protein (Chen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There is a significant decrease in Nrp2 protein in Nrp2+/− cochleae.
source: To determine if this is the case in SGNs, we examined protein levels by Western blot and found a significant decrease in Nrp in Nrp2+/− cochleae (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: An increased percentage of SGN fibers extended into the OHC region in Nrp2+/− cochleae.
source: As expected, an increased percentage of SGN fibers extended into the OHC region in Nrp2+/− cochleae (Figure 4C,D; see arrowheads).
evidence: This is a direct observation from sparse SGN labeling data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: There is nearly a 40% increase in type II-like SGN fibers in Nrp2+/− cochleae at P1.
source: Results indicated nearly a 40% increase in type II-like SGN fibers (among the labeled population) in Nrp2+/− cochleae at P1 (Figure 4E), confirming the phenotype observed in embryonic cochleae from Nrp2 mutants.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from sparse SGN labeling data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Nrp2+/− SGN neurites showed a significant increase in the number of filopodial branches.
source: WT and Nrp2+/− SGNs did not show differences in filopodial length (not shown), but Nrp2+/− SGNs neurites did show a significant increase in the number of filopodial branches (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from morphological analysis shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: There were no differences in the percentages of medially or laterally positioned SGNs between Nrp2+/− and WT cochleae.
source: We tracked over 1500 SGNs between Nrp2+/− and WT cochleae and found no differences in the percentages of medially or laterally positioned SGNs (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from SGN tracking data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Nrp2 mediates an inhibitory signal within SGN fibers that decreases terminal complexity and prevents fibers from extending processes into the OHC region.
source: These data support the hypothesis that Nrp2 mediates an inhibitory signal within SGN fibers that decreases terminal complexity and prevents fibers from extending processes into the OHC region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotypes in Nrp2 mutant mice.

claim: Nrp2 does not appear to play a role in the patterning of fibers within the IHC region.
source: However, Nrp2 does not appear to play a role in the patterning of fibers within the IHC region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of differences in medial/lateral positioning of SGNs.

claim: Synapse numbers for both IHCs and OHCs were unchanged between WT and Nrp2+/− mutants at P8 and P21.
source: Surprisingly, synapse numbers for both IHCs and OHCs were unchanged between WT and Nrp2+/− mutants (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from ribbon synapse counting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: No difference in number of ribbon synapses was observed in Nrp2−/− cochleae at P21 compared to controls.
source: For these studies, we were also able to examine both cochleae from one surviving Nrp2−/− mouse at P21. However, no difference in number of ribbon synapses (as compared to controls) was observed in these cochleae either.
evidence: This is a direct observation from ribbon synapse counting data.

claim: Assessment of hearing sensitivity by auditory brainstem response indicated no significant differences between WT and Nrp2+/− mice.
source: Consistent with this result, assessment of hearing sensitivity by auditory brainstem response indicated no significant differences between WT and Nrp2+/− mice (not shown).
evidence: This is a direct statement about functional hearing assessment.

claim: Although there was a small increase in type II projections in Nrp2+/− cochleae at P21 as compared to controls, the difference was not significant.
source: Although there was a small increase in type II projections in Nrp2+/− cochleae as compared to controls, the difference was not significant.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the quantification of type II projections at P21.

claim: Innervation is normal in adult Nrp2+/− cochleae.
source: Overall, these results suggest that innervation is normal in adult Nrp2+/− cochleae.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of differences in synapse numbers and hearing sensitivity.

claim: After birth, the cochlea goes through a significant phase of synaptic pruning in conjunction with innervation by olivocochlear efferents.
source: However, after birth, the cochlea goes through a significant phase of synaptic pruning in conjunction with innervation by olivocochlear efferents (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The synaptic pruning mechanism is independent of Nrp2 and can act to correct any increases in SGN fibers in the OHC region.
source: Therefore, it seems likely that this pruning mechanism is independent of Nrp2 and can therefore act to correct any increases in SGN fibers in the OHC region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the normalization of innervation patterns in adult Nrp2 mutants.

claim: Sema3c mRNA is detectable in the SG, in the greater epithelial ridge of the cochlear epithelium, and very faintly in the IHC and OHCs.
source: Sema3b (not shown) and Sema3c showed a nearly identical expression pattern; mRNA was detectable in the SG, in the greater epithelial ridge (GER; non-sensory cells) of the cochlear epithelium, and very faintly in the IHC and OHCs (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Sema3d mRNA was not detectable in the SG but was detectable in an unusual striping pattern in the GER.
source: Sema3d mRNA was not detectable in the SG but was detectable in an unusual striping pattern in the GER (Figure 6D–F; see the arrow in Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Richardson et al. did not detect Sema3g expression in the E14.5 cochlea.
source: In situ hybridization for Sema3g was not performed, but Richardson et al. did not detect Sema3g expression in the E14.5 cochlea (Richardson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Sema3f mRNA is expressed in a pattern highly suggestive of a role in activating Nrp2.
source: In contrast with these results, Sema3f mRNA is expressed in a pattern highly suggestive of a role in activating Nrp2 (Figure 6G–N).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6G-N.

claim: At E16.5, Sema3f transcripts are detectable in the apical, middle, and basal turns of the cochlea in a pattern that is distinct from the other Sema3s examined.
source: At E14.5 (not shown) and E16.5, Sema3f transcripts were detectable in the apical, middle, and basal turns of the cochlea in a pattern that is distinct from the other Sema3s we examined (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Sema3f expression is present in two regions of the duct: an extreme medial region near the junction with Reissner's membrane and in a lateral domain that correlates with the developing sensory epithelium.
source: Expression of Sema3f is present in two regions of the duct: an extreme medial region near the junction with Reissner's membrane and in a lateral domain that correlates with the developing sensory epithelium.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data.

claim: Sema3f appears to be expressed in a domain of cells that includes OHCs, pillar cells, Dieters' cells, and Henson's cells.
source: At higher magnification, Sema3f appears to be expressed in a domain of cells that includes OHCs, pillar cells (PCs), Dieters' cells, and Henson's cells (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The Sema3f expression domain has a sharp medial boundary that appears to correlate with the junction between the IHC and OHC regions.
source: Moreover, the domain has a sharp medial boundary that appears to correlate with the junction between the IHC and OHC regions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data.

claim: Sema3f expression clearly overlaps with the OHC region and is completely absent from the IHC region.
source: The merged image demonstrates that Sema3f expression clearly overlaps with the OHC region and is completely absent from the IHC region.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data with immunostaining shown in Figure 6J-L.

claim: The sharp medial boundary of Sema3f expression appears to precisely correlate with the limiting extension of developing SGN processes.
source: In addition, the sharp medial boundary appears to precisely correlate with the limiting extension of developing SGN processes.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data with immunostaining.

claim: At postnatal day 0, Sema3f expression in the cochlea is diminished and the distribution pattern has changed.
source: At postnatal day 0 (P0), Sema3f expression in the cochlea is diminished and the distribution pattern has changed.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data.

claim: At the apex at P0, Sema3f is detectable in the PCs and faintly present in nearby supporting cells.
source: At the apex, Sema3f is detectable in the PCs and faintly present in nearby supporting cells, while at the cochlear base, Sema3f expression is limited to just the outer PCs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data.

claim: At the cochlear base at P0, Sema3f expression is limited to just the outer PCs.
source: At the apex, Sema3f is detectable in the PCs and faintly present in nearby supporting cells, while at the cochlear base, Sema3f expression is limited to just the outer PCs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data.

claim: At P5, Sema3f was not detectable in the cochlear epithelium.
source: At P5, Sema3f was not detectable in the cochlear epithelium (not shown).
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data.

claim: Sema3F protein is distributed in a spatial and temporal pattern consistent with a role in activating Nrp2 on SGNs.
source: These data suggest that Sema3F protein is distributed in a spatial and temporal pattern consistent with a role in activating Nrp2 on SGNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Sema3f expression pattern.

claim: SGN processes from cochleae treated with Sema3F-Fc showed mostly blunt endings with very little branching.
source: In contrast, SGN processes from cochleae treated with Sema3F-Fc showed mostly blunt endings with very little branching (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from cochlear explant culture experiments shown in Figure 7B,D.

claim: For experiments initiated at either E15.5 or E16.5, the addition of Sema3F-Fc led to nearly a 50% decrease in the number of SGN branch tips.
source: For experiments initiated at either E15.5 or E16.5, the addition of Sema3F-Fc led to nearly a 50% decrease in the number of SGN branch tips.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from cochlear explant culture experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Exposure to Sema3F-Fc did not decrease the number of processes that reached the IHC region.
source: While exposure to Sema3F-Fc did not decrease the number of processes that reached the IHC region (Figure 7F–G), there was an obvious decrease in the number of branched protrusions per process (Figure 7G,I).
evidence: This is a direct observation from cochlear explant culture experiments with sparse SGN labeling shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the number of branches per SGN process in the presence of Sema3F-Fc.
source: Results indicate a significant reduction in the number of branches in the presence of Sema3F-Fc (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from cochlear explant culture experiments shown in Figure 7K.

claim: A localized source of Sema3F in the OHC region acts to activate Nrp2 in SGN growth cones leading to decreased complexity and extension.
source: These data are consistent with the hypothesis that a localized source of Sema3F in the OHC region acts to activate Nrp2 in SGN growth cones leading to decreased complexity and extension.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cochlear explant culture experiments.

claim: Sema3f−/− cochleae showed an increased percentage of SGN processes in the OHC region.
source: As predicted, Sema3f−/− cochleae showed an increased percentage of SGN processes in the OHC region.
evidence: This is a direct observation from sparse SGN labeling in Sema3f mutant mice.

claim: The increase in crossing processes in Sema3f−/− cochleae was comparable to that observed in Nrp2+/− heterozygotes.
source: Interestingly, when we quantified the increase in crossing processes in Sema3f−/− cochleae (Figure 8C), we found that it was comparable to that observed in Nrp2+/− heterozygotes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between Sema3f and Nrp2 mutant phenotypes shown in Figure 8C and Figure 4.

claim: No changes in either HC or SGN density were observed in Sema3f−/− cochleae.
source: Compared to littermate controls, we did not observe any changes in either HC or SGN density in Sema3f−/− cochleae (Figure 8D–G), suggesting the extraneous SGN processes in the OHC region are not a secondary effect of other cochlear changes.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from HC and SGN counting data shown in Figure 8D-G.

claim: Analysis of adult Sema3f−/− cochleae indicated no differences in the density of ribbon synapses between control and Sema3f−/−.
source: To determine whether the increase in OHC innervation in Sema3f−/− cochleae led to increased ribbon synapse formation, we used the same approach as for Nrp2-deficient cochleae (Figure 5). Results indicated no differences in the density of ribbon synapses between control and Sema3f−/−.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from ribbon synapse counting data shown in Figure 8H-L.

claim: Synaptic pruning events that occur following innervation probably lead to a correction in the number of SGN fibers present in the OHC region in Sema3f mutants.
source: As was suggested for the Nrp2 animals, these results suggest that synaptic pruning events that occur following innervation probably lead to a correction in the number of SGN fibers present in the OHC region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the normalization of synapse numbers in adult Sema3f mutants.

claim: Sema3F acts as a ligand for Nrp2 to control SGN extension into the OHC region during development.
source: These data support a model in which Sema3F acts as a ligand for Nrp2 to control SGN extension into the OHC region during development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from Nrp2 and Sema3f mutants and in vitro experiments.

claim: Intracellular-signaling events that occur as a result of Sema3f/Nrp2 interactions depend entirely on the presence of Plexin-A3.
source: It was shown previously that intracellular-signaling events that occur as a result of Sema3f/Nrp2 interactions depend entirely on the presence of Plexin-A3 (Yaron et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Plxna3 mRNA is distributed in the cochleovestibular ganglion at E11.5 and in the SGNs at E13.5 and E15.5.
source: In situ hybridization data from the Allen Brain Atlas Website clearly show Plxna3 mRNA distribution in the cochleovestibular ganglion at E11.5 and in the SGNs at E13.5 and E15.5 (http://developingmouse.brain-map.org/gene/show/18610) (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statement about data from the Allen Brain Atlas, shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plxna3 antisense probes indicated broad expression in SGNs in both the apical and basal regions of the cochlea at E16.5.
source: Consistent with the Allen Brain Atlas, Plxna3 antisense probes indicated broad expression in SGNs in both the apical and basal regions of the cochlea (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 9A-C.

claim: No obvious differences in Plxna3 mRNA were detected within the SGN population.
source: Using differential interference contrast to closely examine the SGNs (Figure 9D–F), we did not detect any obvious differences in Plxna3 mRNA within the population, suggesting uniform expression of Plxna3.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 9D-F.

claim: Plexin-A3 protein is visible broadly in the SGN processes at E16.5 in a pattern similar to that of Tuj1.
source: At low magnification, Plexin-A3 protein is visible broadly in the SGN processes in a pattern similar to that of Tuj1 (Figure 9G–I).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 9G-I.

claim: Plexin-A3 expression in fibers extending beyond the IHC region is markedly reduced by comparison with substantially higher levels in fibers that terminate near IHCs.
source: However, at high-magnification, Plexin-A3 expression in fibers extending beyond the IHC region is markedly reduced by comparison with substantially higher levels in fibers that terminate near IHCs (Figure 9G–L).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 9G-L.

claim: Plexin-A3 expression on fibers located in the OHC region is detectable only on sparse numbers of SGNs as small puncta.
source: But, Plexin-A3 expression on fibers located in the OHC region is detectable only on sparse numbers of SGNs as small puncta (arrowheads).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Plexin-A3 may act as an Nrp2 co-receptor in SGNs.
source: These data suggest that Plexin-A3 may act as an Nrp2 co-receptor in SGNs, and that differences in Plexin-A3 protein levels could modulate Sema3F-mediated repulsion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Plexin-A3 expression pattern and known signaling mechanisms.

claim: Differences in Plexin-A3 protein levels could modulate Sema3F-mediated repulsion.
source: These data suggest that Plexin-A3 may act as an Nrp2 co-receptor in SGNs, and that differences in Plexin-A3 protein levels could modulate Sema3F-mediated repulsion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential Plexin-A3 expression in type I vs type II-like fibers.

claim: Repulsive signaling mediated by Sema3F in the OHC region and Nrp2 in SGNs controls, at least in part, the number of SGN fibers that terminate on OHCs.
source: In these studies, we demonstrate that repulsive signaling mediated by Sema3F in the OHC region and Nrp2 in SGNs controls, at least in part, the number of SGN fibers that terminate on OHCs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: The embryonic OHC region maintains a compartment of Sema3F protein expression, which activates Nrp2 receptors expressed on SGNs leading to retraction of processes.
source: Our findings support a model in which the embryonic OHC region maintains a compartment of Sema3F protein expression, which activates Nrp2 receptors expressed on SGNs leading to retraction of processes (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined experimental findings.

claim: Since the Sema3F inhibitory signal is restricted to the OHC domain, this interaction would enforce contacts between SGN fibers and IHCs.
source: Since this inhibitory signal is restricted to the OHC domain, this interaction would enforce contacts between SGN fibers and IHCs.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the spatial restriction of Sema3F expression.

claim: Type I SGNs were still observed even in the complete absence of either Nrp2 or Sema3f.
source: Type I SGNs were still observed even in the complete absence of either Nrp2 or Sema3f.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the mutant analysis.

claim: Compensatory guidance mechanisms are likely in place to ensure that most type I SGNs terminate on IHCs.
source: First, it is reasonable to assume that compensatory guidance mechanisms are in place to ensure that most type I SGNs terminate on IHCs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the incomplete penetrance of the mutant phenotype.

claim: Ephrin-A5/Epha4 signaling may also act to repel type I SGNs from OHCs.
source: In addition, it was recently shown that ephrin-A5/Epha4 signaling may also act to repel type I SGNs from OHCs (Defourny et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The extent to which ephrin-A5/Epha4 factors are involved in targeting events during embryonic development remains uncertain.
source: These studies, however, were limited to early postnatal and adult cochlear samples, thus, the extent to which these factors are involved in targeting events during embryonic development remains uncertain.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research.

claim: Some SGNs may be initially committed to a type I fate while others rely on target-based interactions to determine their phenotype.
source: This hypothesis might be consistent with the idea that some SGNs are initially committed to a type I fate while others rely on target-based interactions to determine their phenotype.
evidence: This is speculation about the heterogeneity of SGN determination mechanisms.

claim: Despite the presence of additional type II-like processes in Nrp2+/− cochleae at birth, analysis of adult animals indicated a normal number of type II SGNs and hearing sensitivity.
source: As discussed, despite the presence of additional type II-like processes in Nrp2+/− cochleae at birth, analysis of adult animals indicated a normal number of type II SGNs and hearing sensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from postnatal analysis.

claim: The additional type II-like fibers observed at birth are most likely eliminated over time.
source: These results suggest that the additional type II-like fibers observed at birth are most likely eliminated over time and the factors that mediate this recovery are unknown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the normalization of innervation patterns in adults.

claim: Eph/ephrin signaling might be involved in synaptic pruning-based refinements postnatally.
source: Given that 'mature' type I/type II SGN patterns are established by P0 (Figure 2) and that HC ribbon synapses are visible by P0 (Huang et al., 2012), it could be that Eph/ephrin signaling might be involved in synaptic pruning-based refinements postnatally.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms for postnatal refinement.

claim: Programmed cell death may contribute to the final innervation pattern in postnatal gerbil.
source: In addition, programmed cell death may also contribute to the final innervation pattern, as apoptosis in SGNs has been reported in the postnatal gerbil (Echteler et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous research in gerbil.

claim: Apoptosis does not play a significant role in shaping cochlear innervation during mouse development.
source: Therefore, while we cannot rule it out entirely, we would not predict that apoptosis plays a significant role in shaping cochlear innervation during development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of observed apoptosis in the authors' experiments.

claim: Type I and type II SGNs may differentially express or target Plexin-A co-receptors.
source: We are currently in favor of the model that type I and type II SGNs differentially express or target Plexin-A co-receptors, as the absence of these obligatory co-receptors could effectively inactive the Sema3F-Nrp2 inhibitory interaction.
evidence: This is a proposed model to explain how type II SGNs can extend into the OHC region despite expressing Nrp2.

claim: Plexin-A1 and Plexin-A3 proteins were localized to the SGNs previously.
source: Plexin-A1 and Plexin-A3 proteins were localized to the SGNs previously (Murakami et al., 2001; Katayama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Plxna3 mRNA is broadly expressed by the SGNs.
source: Here, we found Plxna3 mRNA broadly expressed by the SGNs and Plexin-A3 protein enriched in putative type I SGNs (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a direct observation from in situ hybridization and immunostaining data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Plexin-A3 protein is enriched in putative type I SGNs.
source: Here, we found Plxna3 mRNA broadly expressed by the SGNs and Plexin-A3 protein enriched in putative type I SGNs (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Where type I or II SGNs ultimately terminate may depend on Plexin-A3 protein levels.
source: While these data suggest that where type I or II SGNs ultimately terminate may depend on Plexin-A3 protein levels, a more careful analysis of the Plexin-A3 distribution and function is needed.
evidence: This is speculation based on the differential Plexin-A3 protein distribution.

claim: GATA transcription factors have been shown to regulate Sema expression.
source: GATA transcription factors have been shown previously to regulate Sema expression and are known players in inner ear morphogenesis and wiring (Lepore et al., 2006; Kodo et al., 2009; Appler and Lu, 2013), so perhaps one role of GATAs in the inner ear is to regulate Sema3 levels.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: One role of GATAs in the inner ear may be to regulate Sema3 levels.
source: GATA transcription factors have been shown previously to regulate Sema expression and are known players in inner ear morphogenesis and wiring (Lepore et al., 2006; Kodo et al., 2009; Appler and Lu, 2013), so perhaps one role of GATAs in the inner ear is to regulate Sema3 levels.
evidence: This is speculation based on known roles of GATA factors.

claim: Loss of Prox1 or Fgfr3 signaling led to increases in OHC innervation.
source: Other clues related to this matter may come from previous findings where either the loss of Prox1 or Fgfr3 signaling led to increases in OHC innervation (Puligilla et al., 2007; Fritzsch et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Prox1 may control the expression of factors such as Sema3f.
source: It is possible, therefore, that Prox1 controls the expression of factors such as Sema3f or that the local distribution of the different Sema3s is controlled by morphogens such as Fgfs.
evidence: This is speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The local distribution of the different Sema3s may be controlled by morphogens such as Fgfs.
source: It is possible, therefore, that Prox1 controls the expression of factors such as Sema3f or that the local distribution of the different Sema3s is controlled by morphogens such as Fgfs.
evidence: This is speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms.
